slides.title: Greedy algorithms and heuristics
slides.main: At every step take the best option available right now: when it works, it is the most elegant code there is.

captions: At every step we take the best option available right now
We never revisit choices or plan ahead
Sometimes it is optimal, sometimes it misleads: here, picking a path by sum

slides.title: Activity selection
slides.sub: Maximum events without overlaps, one hall
slides.main: The right greedy rule is to sort by end time: free the hall as soon as possible.

Sort by end time to free the hall as early as possible

slides.title: Huffman code
slides.sub: Lossless compression: frequent short, rare long
slides.main: Every step is locally best, and together they give an optimal prefix code.

slides.title: Short jobs first
slides.main: Sort by increasing duration: a short job at the front cuts the wait of everyone behind it.

captions: Job queue 5, 2, 8, 1: total waiting time 27
Short jobs first: everyone waits less than behind a long job
Waiting dropped from 27 to 12, the minimum

slides.title: Why greedy works
slides.main: Greed is optimal with the greedy choice property and optimal substructure.

captions: The greedy step is optimal because estimates can no longer improve
The lightest edge that closes no cycle is in some minimum spanning tree
The cheapest edge leaving the tree is also safe
Merging the two rarest symbols is proven by exchange

slides.title: Sorting plus two pointers
slides.sub: Children with appetites and cookies with sizes
slides.main: Sorting creates an order where the greedy choice is obvious, and two pointers carry it out in linear time.

captions: Appetites 1, 2, 3 and cookies of size 1, 1, 2: maximize happy children
The least demanding child gets the smallest fitting cookie
Skip a cookie that is too small: it fits no one
Two pointers plus greed: sort, then one pass

slides.title: Two knapsacks
slides.sub: Divisibility of items decides the method
slides.main: Before choosing an algorithm, ask what freedoms the data gives you.

captions: Items (weight / value): 10 / 60, 20 / 100, 30 / 120; capacity 50
Cutting allowed: by value per kg, 60 + 100 + 80 (two thirds of the third) = 240, optimal
No cutting: greedy takes the first two, 160, and the third does not fit
Better the second and third: 100 + 120 = 220; DP is needed

slides.title: When exact is unaffordable
slides.sub: A salesman with a hundred cities
slides.main: Heuristics and approximation algorithms give good answers in acceptable time.

captions: Salesman: visit all cities on the shortest closed route; exact solving grows factorially
Heuristic: from the current city, go to the nearest unvisited one
Fast and usually decent, but no guarantees; for guarantees, use approximation

frames.text: within a factor of two: a guarantee of an approximation algorithm

slides.title: Guarantee versus hope
slides.main: “Predictably good on any data”: look for an approximation algorithm; “usually good”: a heuristic is enough.

captions: A heuristic is a sensible strategy with no promises
An approximation algorithm promises: within, say, 2x of optimal, and it is proven
Walking the minimum spanning tree gives a route at most twice the optimal
